entries.meaning: Delighted by Jambavan's words, Hanuman asks his companions to endure on roots and fruit until he returns after seeing Sita. Holding Rama in his heart, he bounds from a mountain so forcefully that it sinks toward the netherworld, and flies like Rama's unfailing arrow. The Ocean sends Mainaka to ease Rama's messenger, but Hanuman only touches and salutes the mountain: there can be no rest before Rama's work is done.

The gods send Surasa, mother of serpents, to test Hanuman's strength and intelligence. Claiming him as food, she refuses passage. Hanuman promises to enter her mouth after reporting Sita's news; when she persists and enlarges her mouth, he doubles his body at every stage. At one hundred yojanas he instantly becomes tiny, enters and exits her mouth, and bows. Satisfied that she has perceived his wisdom and strength, Surasa blesses him to complete Rama's work.

Hanuman kills the sea-demoness who seizes flying creatures by their shadows, crosses the ocean, and surveys Lanka from a mountain. He sees a nearly impregnable golden city crowded with mansions, markets, streets, armies, many-shaped demons, gardens, pools, celestial women, wrestlers, and guards; wicked demons feast on many creatures. Tulsidas says their story is told because Rama's arrow will become the holy ford through which they leave their bodies and gain their destined state. Seeing the guards, Hanuman resolves to enter at night in a minute form.

In a mosquito-sized form Hanuman approaches Lanka, but her guardian Lankini challenges him and claims every thief as her food. One blow leaves her bleeding and reeling. Recovering, she joins her hands and recalls Brahma's sign: when a monkey's blow disables her, the demons' destruction is near. Calling herself greatly blessed to see Rama's messenger, she declares that all pleasures of heaven and liberation together cannot equal even a moment of holy company.

Lankini bids Hanuman enter while holding Ayodhya's king in his heart, for Rama's grace turns poison to nectar, enemies to friends, the ocean to a calf's hoofprint, fire to coolness, and Meru to dust. In a tiny form Hanuman searches innumerable houses and warriors, including Ravana's wondrous palace, but does not see Vaidehi. Then he notices a distinct shrine of Hari, a house marked with Rama's weapons and fresh clusters of sacred basil, and rejoices.

Wondering how a good person can live in demon-filled Lanka, Hanuman hears Vibhishana wake and remember Rama. Recognizing a virtuous man, he assumes a Brahmin's form and speaks. Vibhishana bows, asks his story, and wonders whether he is a servant of Hari—or Rama himself, lover of the lowly, come to bless him. Hanuman tells Rama's whole story and his own name; both bodies thrill and their minds sink into remembrance of Rama's virtues.

Vibhishana describes life in Lanka as a tongue surrounded by teeth and asks whether the Lord of the solar line will ever pity an orphan like him. Born in a tamasic body, he claims no practice or love of Rama's lotus feet, yet Hanuman's arrival gives hope because saints meet only through Hari's grace. Hanuman replies that the Lord always loves servants and humbly calls monkeys fickle and deficient—yet Rama has shown grace even to him. Remembering that grace, his eyes fill with tears.

Those who knowingly forget such a Master must suffer. Speaking Rama's virtues gives Hanuman and Vibhishana indescribable peace. Vibhishana explains where Janaka's daughter is kept, and Hanuman asks to see Mother Janaki. Following his directions, Hanuman reaches the Ashoka grove and silently bows to Sita. Emaciated, with matted hair in a single braid, she repeats Rama's virtues; her eyes rest on her own feet while her mind is absorbed in Rama's lotus feet. Hanuman is deeply distressed by her misery.

Hidden among leaves, Hanuman deliberates as Ravana arrives surrounded by adorned women. Ravana tries conciliation, gifts, threats, and division, promising to make all queens—including Mandodari—Sita's attendants if she looks at him once. Placing a blade of grass between them and remembering Rama, Sita says a firefly cannot make a lotus bloom and asks the shameless abductor how he can compare himself to Rama, the sun. Enraged by her harsh words, Ravana draws his sword.

Ravana threatens to cut off Sita's head unless she obeys immediately. Sita declares that either Rama's dark, lotus-garland-like arms will embrace her neck or Ravana's dreadful sword will strike it. She asks the cool, keen Chandrahāsa blade to end the fire of separation from Rama. Ravana rushes to kill her, but Mandodari restrains him with policy. He orders the demonesses to terrorize Sita and gives her one month to submit before death, then returns to his palace while the demonesses assume hideous forms.
